summary: Reports a systematic survey of two decades of proposals for supporting mobility on the Internet. It tries to give an overall picture of the solution space and identifies remaining issues in providing efficient, ubiquitous mobility support globally. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When you carry your phone around, the network has to keep finding you. This paper collects all the ideas people have tried for that and points out what still is not solved.

questions: what are the main approaches to internet mobility
how do mobility protocols handle changing ip addresses
what is triangle routing in mobile ip
why has mobility support been difficult to deploy
subtitle: Two decades of solutions for keeping mobile devices connected

tldr.problem: Mobile devices need to stay connected as they move between networks, but IP addresses change and need to be tracked.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys 18 major mobility protocols developed since the early 1990s, analyzing how they separate stable identifiers from changing locators to solve this fundamental routing problem.
tldr.outcome: Most solutions use either routing-based or mapping-based approaches, each with trade-offs in scalability, deployment complexity, and backward compatibility.

facts.label: Core problem
facts.value: Mapping changing IP addresses to stable identities

facts.label: Primary barrier
facts.value: Protocol complexity and lack of deployment incentives

today: RFC 6301 is an Informational RFC published in July 2011. Mobility support on the Internet remains a landscape of coexisting approaches rather than a single standardized solution. Mobile IP and its variants see deployment in some carrier networks, but many proposed solutions have seen only research or limited real-world deployment. The explosion of mobile device usage since 2011 has kept mobility a live research area.

sections.title: Internet Mobility: The Core Problem
sections.content:
Supporting mobility on the Internet is fundamentally about delivering packets to a moving destination. The challenge arises because IP addresses serve two purposes: they identify where a device is (locator) and who it is (identifier). When a mobile node moves, its locator changes, but other nodes need to keep reaching it using a stable identifier.

The RFC surveys 20 years of research and standardization efforts starting from the early 1990s through 2009, examining how different protocols solve this core problem. Only a few have been widely deployed; most remain research proposals or limited deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your mailbox needs to know where you live so it can deliver letters. If you move houses, the mailbox still needs to find you, but your address changes.

sections.title: The Three Essential Components
sections.content:
Every mobility solution requires three basic elements. First, a stable Identifier: something topologically independent that does not change when the mobile moves, such as a home address, domain name, or cryptographic key. Second, a Locator, which is the IP address representing the mobile's current attachment point to the network. Third, a Mapping between the identifier and the current locator, stored at a Rendezvous Point.

Solutions fall into two categories. Type-1 uses DNS to provide current IP address information (the locator can be looked up by name). Type-2 uses a stable IP address as the identifier and maintains a mapping at a home location that forwards packets to the current locator. All of type-2 faces the challenge of triangle routing: packets from a correspondent node must go through the home location even after the home knows where the mobile is.
sections.plainLanguage: You need three things: a name that does not change (like your name), where you are right now (your address), and a record somewhere that matches your name to your current address.

sections.title: Survey of 18 Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC describes 18 mobility support protocols proposed between 1991 and 2009, ranging from early campus-scale solutions to global-scale protocols. Early proposals like Columbia (1991) and VIP (1991) introduced core concepts. Mobile IP, standardized by the IETF in 1996 for IPv4 and 2004 for IPv6, became the reference point for many discussions. Other major protocols include HMIP (hierarchical local mobility), NEMO (network mobility for moving groups), Cellular IP and HAWAII (local domain solutions), Host Identity Protocol (cryptographic identifiers), and emerging approaches like LISP-Mobility that leverage Internet routing infrastructure.

The document also covers network-based approaches like Proxy Mobile IP (PMIP), where the network handles mobility transparently without requiring mobile devices to participate in signaling, and application-layer solutions using SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers have tried many different approaches: some make routers smart about mobility, some use a home base to forward packets, some use DNS, and some build mobility into the application layer instead.

sections.title: Design Dimensions and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five key dimensions along which mobility solutions vary. First, routing-based versus mapping-based: routing updates the network about a mobile's location (broadcast-based or path-based), or a mapping service tracks the mobile at a single point. Routing-based approaches scale poorly to large networks with many mobiles but provide direct paths. Mapping-based approaches scale better but risk triangle routing.

Second, mobility awareness: solutions differ in whether the correspondent node, the mobile, the network, or combinations thereof must participate in mobility signaling. Hiding mobility from legacy nodes (Design 1) sacrifices triangle routing optimization but enables unilateral deployment. Hiding mobility from both mobile and correspondent (Design 2, like PMIP) requires network infrastructure upgrades. Making both ends mobility-aware (Design 3, like DNS-based E2E) simplifies infrastructure but requires software support.

Third, operator-controlled versus user-controlled: cellular networks follow an operator-controlled model where network entities manage all signaling, while most Internet protocols assume user-controlled devices that update their location themselves. Fourth, local versus global scale: some protocols optimize for performance in small domains (local mobility management), while others target global Internet scale.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol makes different choices: does the network tell routers, or does a central database keep track? Do old devices need to help, or can new ones handle it alone? Does the phone company control it, or does your device?

sections.title: Remaining Challenges and Open Issues
sections.content:
Despite two decades of effort, significant deployment and design challenges persist. Few protocols have reached commercial deployment at scale. Complexity is a barrier: most protocols include performance optimizations and security mechanisms (IPsec, IKE) that make them difficult to implement correctly.

Session continuity presents an ongoing challenge, particularly for long-lived connections like voice calls that survive handovers. While routing-based protocols handle this naturally (the IP address never changes), other approaches require stable upper-layer identifiers or TCP/transport modifications. Simultaneous movements—where both ends are mobile—require rendezvous points in almost all designs.

Backward compatibility creates fundamental tensions. Supporting legacy devices that do not implement mobility protocols requires hiding mobility from them, adding complexity. As mobile devices become dominant, the value of backward compatibility may diminish.

Finally, interoperability between heterogeneous systems remains problematic. A Mobile IP device cannot communicate with an HIP-only device while both benefit from mobility support. The RFC suggests this may require something analogous to how IP merged earlier networks: a new layer of indirection to translate between different mobility paradigms.
sections.plainLanguage: Big unsolved problems: nothing has really become standard and easy to use, voice calls drop during handovers, devices moving at the same time are hard to handle, and different solutions do not work together.
